slides.title: Remember: We Built Adders
points: A half-adder adds two bits: the sum is an exclusive OR, the carry is an AND
1× 8-bit adder = 8× 1-bit adders that are connected properly: 40 gates, about 80 transistors
Arranged in a 3D grid, that's a cube of about 125 nm × 125 nm × 125 nm

slides.title: CPU Architectures Work with Two Main Illusions

groups.heading: Instruction set architecture
points: ISAs assume that instructions are executed in sequence
Processor hardware is more elaborate, but ensures that the overall behavior matches sequential execution

groups.heading: Linear memory model
points: We assume that memory is simply a very large byte array
Hardware is much more elaborate, but makes sure that its outside behavior matches the linear memory model

slides.after: In the lectures, you will see x86-64; in the second exercise, you apply the concepts to ARMv8.

slides.title: Let's build a simple CPU that works on 4-bit numbers
slides.lead: Computing is just mathematics (that's what Leibniz said already!). Simple idea, in principle…
points: Construct an adding circuit
Construct multiplier, subtractor, divider circuits: let's say we have 4 such units!
Add memory for inputs and outputs
Wire all these components together…

slides.title: We also want to select which of these four functions to perform!

callout.text: In modern processors, we call this an Arithmetic/Logic Unit (ALU)

first 4-bit number   second 4-bit number
        |                   |
  +-----+------+------+-----+
  | add | mult | sub  | div | <- function
  +-----+------+------+-----+    select
               |                 (2 bits)
         output / result

slides.title: Designing a Simple Instruction Set Architecture
slides.lead: Here's the CPU hardware we have: 4 memory slots and 2 data registers of 4 bits each, and an ALU that can add and subtract.
items: How many bits do we need to address four memory slots?
How many bits do we need to address two registers?
How many bits do we need to encode five instructions?

slides.title: Our Instruction Set: 5 Instructions
rows: Load from memory address xx (M[xx]) into register y (R[y])
Add the contents of R[0] and R[1] and store the result in R[x]
Subtract the contents of R[0] from R[1] and store the result in R[x]
Insert the 4-bit number n into M[xx]

slides.title: Writing a Program for our ISA
slides.code:
// Machine-level program that adds 7 and 8
Insert 7 into M[00]:      100 0111 00
Insert 8 into M[01]:      ?
Load from M[00] to R[0]:  ?
Load from M[01] to R[1]:  ?
Add registers into R[0]:  ?
Store R[0] into M[10]:    ?

slides.title: Writing a Program for our ISA: Done!
slides.code:
// Machine-level program that adds 7 and 8
Insert 7 into M[00]:      100 0111 00
Insert 8 into M[01]:      100 1000 01
Load from M[00] to R[0]:  000 00 0
Load from M[01] to R[1]:  000 01 1
Add registers into R[0]:  010 0
Store R[0] into M[10]:    001 0 10
points: Memory afterwards: M[00] = 7, M[01] = 8, M[10] = 15
Registers afterwards: R[0] = 15 (it held 7 before the add), R[1] = 8

slides.title: What if we write the program in this way?
points: The encoding of this machine-level program is unique!
We could say that this is the 611'097'513'226th program of our ISA
So this means that programs themselves are just numbers…

slides.title: Reading the Bits: One by One
slides.lead: Let's read machine code one bit at a time…
defs: could be load, store, add or subtract. Let's see the next bit.
could be load or store. Let's see the next bit.
ah, this must be load. Expecting 3 more bits to complete the instruction.
aha! This is a load from M[01] to R[1]. Done. Next instruction please!

aside.alt: A scuba diver under water makes the OK sign with one hand

slides.title: Another Computer Program
points: Note that everything here is again just binary. So we can use our digital circuits to actually process all of this!

aside.code:
Load   M[xx] -> R[y]         000 xx y
Store  R[x] -> M[yy]         001 x yy
Add    R[0] + R[1] -> R[x]   010 x
Sub    R[1] - R[0] -> R[x]   011 x
Insert n -> M[xx]            100 nnnn xx

slides.title: Another Computer Program: Decoded
slides.code:
100 0010 00   Insert 2 into M[00]
100 1000 01   Insert 8 into M[01]
000 00 0      Load M[00] into R[0]
000 01 1      Load M[01] into R[1]
011 0         R[0] = R[1] - R[0]
001 0 00      Store R[0] into M[00]
points: Memory afterwards: M[00] = 6 (it held 2 before), M[01] = 8
Registers afterwards: R[0] = 6, R[1] = 8

slides.title: Self-Test: Write a Multiplier Using Our ISA

aside.code:
Load   M[xx] -> R[y]         000 xx y
Store  R[x] -> M[yy]         001 x yy
Add    R[0] + R[1] -> R[x]   010 x
Sub    R[1] - R[0] -> R[x]   011 x
Insert n -> M[xx]            100 nnnn xx

slides.title: Putting Everything Together

callout.text: How do these components together «run» a computer program?

slides.lead: Memory holds program data and instructions. The CPU runs in a loop; in each cycle:
defs: the control unit decides which instruction is next and fetches it from memory
the CPU finds out what data the instruction needs, and what to do with it
the required data is loaded into the CPU registers
the ALU computes the result of the instruction
the result is sent back and stored in memory

aside.alt: Block diagram of a computer: CPU with control unit, ALU and registers, connected to a memory unit

slides.title: The CPU Clock

callout.text: What are typical CPU clock frequencies?

points: How often this cycle is executed per second is determined by the CPU clock

points.text: However, only few instructions take exactly one clock cycle to execute
sub: Example: on a modern Intel/AMD core, an integer multiplication has a latency of about 3 cycles (on the 2004 Intel Nocona, it was 10)

points: We'll talk more about this when we go into processors after the semester break
slides.after: All of this is (of course) just bits in context…

slides.title: Let's add instruction memory!
slides.lead: «The instruction 100001000b (insert 0010b at memory 00b) is located at memory address 0x100.»
slides.after: We address memory in bytes (0x100 = 256). A 9-bit instruction is rounded up to the next byte: 2 bytes.
slides.notes: Why 0x102? Because we count the bits in the instruction (9 bits) and round up to the next byte (2 bytes).

slides.title: This will become boring fast…
Let's add control flow
slides.lead: A sixth instruction: «continue executing with the instruction at hexadecimal address HHH».
points: Encoding: `101 HHH`
e.g., `101 100` to continue at 0x100. But this would mix binary and hex! Context confusion!!
Better in binary: `101 000100000000`

aside.code:
Load   M[xx] -> R[y]         000 xx y
Store  R[x] -> M[yy]         001 x yy
Add    R[0] + R[1] -> R[x]   010 x
Sub    R[1] - R[0] -> R[x]   011 x
Insert n -> M[xx]            100 nnnn xx
Jump   to address HHH        101 HHH

slides.title: Any Questions / Comments / Doubts / Concerns?
slides.heading: Take-Homes
points: We can selectively switch on our adding circuit, or other types of circuits
The instructions that switch them on or off are binary as well: they are what the processor executes
The processor works with memory that holds instructions and data, and runs in a cycle through all instructions
Very basic control flow can be realized through instruction jumps

slides.title: Putting Everything Together: From Program to Processor
slides.lead: [Remember the bit string](https://hyperdecks.github.io/computersystems/01-information/html/#/45) `11111111 00111111 11111111 00111111`? Bits can also be a machine-level instruction in an x86 processor.
points: e.g., `addq %rax,%rbx`: «Add the two numbers stored in registers %rax and %rbx and store the result in register %rbx.»
Demo: high-level program code to assembly code with [godbolt.org](https://godbolt.org/)
Demo: assembly code to bits with the [online x86 assembler](https://defuse.ca/online-x86-assembler.htm#disassembly)

slides.title: Putting Everything Together
slides.code:
push rbp                    0:  55
mov rbp, rsp                1:  48 89 e5
mov QWORD PTR [rbp-24], rdi 4:  48 89 7d e8
mov rax, QWORD PTR [rbp-24] 8:  48 8b 45 e8
add rax, rax                c:  48 01 c0
mov QWORD PTR [rbp-8], rax  f:  48 89 45 f8
mov rax, QWORD PTR [rbp-8]  13: 48 8b 45 f8
pop rbp                     17: 5d
ret                         18: c3
points: High-level programming language (e.g., C, C#, Go): `long doubleMe(long number) { return number + number; }`
Assembly code (ASM): on the left
Executable machine code, as hex numbers: on the right
…and as one (long) binary number

callout.text: What's the basic problem in this encoding? How would you fix that problem?

aside.code:
00100001

might be  001 00 001
          Run-Jump-Run

might be  00 10 00 01
          Jump-Stop-Jump-Hit

slides.title: Observations
points: More common instructions have shorter encodings
From a given starting position, the decoding of bits to machine instructions is unique
Core issue of the example: the encoding of «Jump» (00) is a prefix of the encoding of «Run» (001)
We say that such codes break the Fano condition

slides.title: Leibniz would say: «Computer programs are very large numbers!»
slides.lead: Each computer program is a binary number, interpreted as executable instructions!
slides.notes: This implies that there are (very many) problems for which no algorithm exists to solve them. Classic example: the Halting Problem.

slides.heading: Take-Homes
points: Not only data is binary, programs are too
Processors run binary code, and compilers translate programs to binary machine code
This translation requires a specification of the instruction set architecture of the target system
This is why you needed to set up the arm-none-eabi toolchain: you compile for a different ISA!

slides.title: Program Compilation and Execution
points: **High-level programming language**: productivity features to simplify writing code; rather generic!
**Assembly code**: textual representation of the machine code with individual instructions; machine-specific!
**Executable machine code**: binary code that is generated from the assembly code and additional data

points: The compiler replaces the division by 8 with a shift by 3 bits
It uses a logical shift for unsigned numbers

slides.title: Let's see it!

callout.text: Why am I not using arm-none-eabi-objdump for notepad.exe?

slides.code:
arm-none-eabi-objdump -d kernel.elf

points: `-d` disassembles the compiled program: instead of translating from human to machine, we translate back to human…
Adding `-S` preserves the structure of the original C code (if this information is available)
With a compiler installed, you can also do this with code compiled for your machine (most probably x86-64), e.g., system programs

slides.title: What are we seeing here?
defs: the memory offset («memory address») of the instruction; 0x8000 is the default load address of 32-bit Raspberry Pi kernels (0x80000 in 64-bit mode), where your program starts
the instruction itself as a hexadecimal number
the mnemonic: a symbolic, human-readable name

aside.alt: Disassembly in a blue terminal: C comments for the GPIO peripheral address, then addresses 8000 to 8010 with hex instructions movw, movt, mov, movt and str

slides.after: Together, all of this is assembly language: a thin layer just above the processing of 0s and 1s.

slides.title: Let's see what this does!
points: Remember the definition: `#define GPIO_BASE 0xFE200000UL`
r3 is 32 bits wide, so r3 contains 8 hex digits: 0x?? 0x?? 0x?? 0x??
slides.caption: [ARM documentation: the Cortex-M3 instruction set](https://developer.arm.com/documentation/dui0552/a/the-cortex-m3-instruction-set/)

slides.title: Let's see what this does!
points: `MOVW Rd, #imm16` copies the value of Operand2 (an «immediate 16-bit value») into register Rd
After `mov r3, #0`: r3 = 0x00 0x00 0x00 0x00
slides.caption: [ARM documentation: the Cortex-M3 instruction set](https://developer.arm.com/documentation/dui0552/a/the-cortex-m3-instruction-set/)

slides.title: Let's see what this does!
points: `MOVT Rd, #imm16` («move top») writes a 16-bit immediate value to the top halfword, Rd[31:16]; it does not affect Rd[15:0]
After `movt r3, #65056`: r3 = 0xFE 0x20 0x00 0x00
slides.caption: [ARM documentation: the Cortex-M3 instruction set](https://developer.arm.com/documentation/dui0552/a/the-cortex-m3-instruction-set/)

slides.title: Assembly language is (has to be!) simple
slides.lead: There are only few types of constructs:
rows: Loading and storing of data from/to memory and registers
Execution of basic logic and arithmetic operations
Jumping (branching) to other addresses to control program flow
slides.after: All high-level constructs (conditionals, loops, function calls, recursion, variables, …) only help programmers write code efficiently. On the machine level, none of them exist directly: machine code is merely sequences of instructions in memory.

slides.title: Exercise… another particularly interesting line…
